assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks (Lamb-Dicke trapping at the magic wavelength, Sr/Yb lattices) opened fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, with direct impact on tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and the prospect of redefining the second. This is precision atomic physics at its best, a clean idea executed to extraordinary quantitative control, and it matches my own sense of what a deep AMO result looks like.
assessment.attribution: The magic-wavelength lattice concept is clearly Katori's, and Jun Ye's group drove the record accuracy and many-body (Fermi-degenerate) clocks. Two laureates is natural. Others, such as Lemonde, Gill and Ludlow, have important contributions, and I am uncertain how a committee would weigh them against the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Many independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB, NIST, NPL) have reproduced and surpassed each other's results over about two decades, and comparisons at the 1e-18 level are routine. Recognition is timely and mature, and the 2005 prize for the frequency comb concerns a related but distinct invention.
uncertainties: I am relying on recalled facts about relative credit between the Tokyo and JILA efforts and have not verified priority details.
Overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes in precision spectroscopy and ion clocks may be seen as partial duplication.
Credit to other clock pioneers outside the supplied names is unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms puts the quantum-classical boundary on the bench, since atoms are shown to interfere over macroscopic distances and times, and it is also a tool for gravimetry, measurements of G and alpha, and tests of the equivalence principle. It is fundamental, simple to explain with images, and has become a precision instrument.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard (first atom interferometers with gratings and light, Mach-Zehnder-type devices), Kasevich and Chu (light-pulse gravimeter, gradiometers) and Borde (Ramsey-Borde interferometer theory and the recoil-shift picture) are all decisive. Steven Chu is not in the supplied names, and he was already honored in 1997 for laser cooling, which complicates a fair configuration. Three names from the list are workable, but ordering of credit is debatable.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many groups worldwide, with commercial and field-deployed gravimeters, and long-baseline instruments in development. The 1997 and 2001 prizes cover neighbouring areas, but the interferometer itself has not been recognized.
uncertainties: Absence of Steven Chu among the credited names weakens a clean attribution.
Priority between Borde, Pritchard and the Kasevich-Chu work is partly a matter of interpretation.
Some fundamental-physics claims, such as dark-energy tests, are still prospective.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: BB84 and the entanglement-based E91 protocol showed that quantum mechanics enables information-theoretically secure key exchange, a conceptually deep result tying the no-cloning theorem and Bell nonlocality to a practical task. It is original and widely taught, and it relates well to the Bell-test physics honored in 2022.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard proposed BB84 and Ekert the entanglement-based scheme, so the three form a coherent, well-known trio. Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea and Deutsch or Mermin contributions complicate priority, though they are not among the credited names.
assessment.maturity: Commercial and satellite-based QKD links exist and the protocols have been demonstrated in many groups. Security under real devices and the practical relevance remain debated, but the underlying idea has been stable since the 1980s and 1990s. The timing is arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as physics rather than computer science or cryptography.
Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding contribution and the nearby 2022 prize may crowd the case.
The nearly identical entry on QKD plus teleportation (separate ballot ID) is not ranked here; the teleportation part would raise credit complications.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, and the HgTe/CdTe experimental observation, opened an entire field of topological band theory. This is a genuine conceptual shift and clearly Nobel-worthy, although it lies outside my own specialty and I defer partly to colleagues in condensed matter.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the original theoretical proposal, and Molenkamp's group delivered the experimental confirmation in HgTe wells together with theory by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang. Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and Fu-Kane-Moore (3D) are not in this credited set, so the configuration may be unfair. Molenkamp is a natural experimental laureate.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed, including ARPES of 3D topological insulators and many follow-on systems, and the Thouless-Haldane-Kosterlitz 2016 prize covers neighbouring topological ideas but not this. Recognition is mature.
uncertainties: Attribution to Zhang, Bernevig, Fu and others remains contested and outside the supplied names.
I defer to condensed-matter colleagues on relative merit against competing topological-matter candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cold atoms in optical lattices act as quantum simulators with controlled many-body physics, such as the observation of the superfluid to Mott insulator transition, and quantum-gas microscopes with single-site resolution. This is fundamental many-body physics realized with atomic precision and well-defined agreement between theory and experiment.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch and others) proposed the Bose-Hubbard realization, Bloch and Greiner carried out the Mott experiment and later developed the microscopes. Jaksch, Cirac and Hansch are important in the early proposal and the experiment, so credit is not fully captured by these three.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced and extended by many groups (Munich, Harvard, MPQ, JILA, Kyoto), and a mature field. Part of the claim, general-purpose quantum simulation, is still developing, but the optical-lattice results are robust.
uncertainties: Overlap with Cirac and Zoller trapped-ion theory and Lukin's Rydberg arrays in other ballot entries.
Credit for the original Mott proposal (Jaksch et al.) and for the Hansch-Greiner experiment lineage is not fully covered.
Possible argument that the best-known results are closer to a decade old than to a pressing recognition need.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The detection of a diffuse high-energy astrophysical neutrino flux and the identification of TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 as sources opened a genuinely new window on the high-energy universe. It is unexpected-nature physics, a km3-scale detector in Antarctic ice, and clearly important.
assessment.attribution: Halzen was the intellectual driver and leader of IceCube, and Karle has had a major role in the detector and in the analysis. A collaboration of hundreds is behind the discovery, and it is difficult to credit a small set. I am uncertain whether the committee would regard two people as sufficient, and Koshiba and Davis were honored in 2002 for earlier neutrino astronomy.
assessment.maturity: The diffuse flux is established at high significance, and source associations are strong for NGC 1068 and the Galactic plane, but source populations are still being resolved. Recognition is arguably timely but may still be a little early for some conclusions.
uncertainties: Attribution within a very large collaboration is hard, and others such as Gaisser, Berezinsky or the AMANDA founders are not credited.
Astroparticle physics is outside my expertise and I defer to colleagues.
Source-level interpretation is still evolving.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cooling macroscopic mechanical resonators to their quantum ground state and entangling them with light or microwaves probes exactly the question I find most compelling, where the boundary lies between the quantum and classical worlds. It is an original and conceptually clear body of work.
assessment.attribution: Cleland and Martinis (quantum ground state of a mechanical resonator, 2010), Teufel (sideband cooling in the microwave domain) and Aspelmeyer (cavity optomechanics, and later entangled and squeezed mechanical states) are all important. Kippenberg, Painter and Regal are also major contributors and not credited, so the set is incomplete and the allocation uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Well reproduced across several platforms, but it is a young field whose applications and the foundational tests of macroscopic superposition are still maturing. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits sits close to the theme and could make recognition seem either synergistic or redundant.
uncertainties: Many comparable contributors, particularly Kippenberg, Painter and Regal, are not credited.
Proximity to the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum phenomena in circuits.
Foundational tests of macroscopic superposition are not yet achieved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light is a clear example of quantum mechanics used to beat a limit, first proposed by Caves for interferometers, observed by Kimble and co-workers, and now implemented in gravitational-wave detectors where it improves sensitivity routinely. It is conceptually elegant and has an impressive, tangible application.
assessment.attribution: Caves made the key theoretical proposal, Kimble's group was among the first to produce squeezed states of light (Slusher, Wu et al. also contributed), and Schnabel led the implementation for GEO600 and later detectors. The roles are distinct and a fair configuration is plausible, but Slusher, Walls, Yuen and others are outside the credited names.
assessment.maturity: Squeezing is operating in LIGO, Virgo and GEO600 as a routine tool, so maturity is high. The 2017 prize for gravitational waves and 2005 prize for quantum optics are neighbours but do not cover squeezing itself.
uncertainties: Priority among the earliest squeezing experiments (Slusher, Kimble, Wu) and the theory (Yuen, Caves) is only partly captured.
Whether the committee sees this as a physics discovery or as an enabling technique.
Recognition may appear to piggyback on the LIGO prize.
